## Highlights

{{< include support/highlights.md >}}
:::

**Abstract**

Separating beat-to-beat (RR) interval variability into vagal-like and sympathetic-like components is an inverse problem that RR alone may not solve uniquely. SPARK (Stochastic Phase-domain Autonomic Reconstruction Kinetics) models two mean-reverting latent drives that modulate an integrate-and-fire pacemaker; conditioning on each interval yields exact continuous-time Kalman filtering over irregular beats, and time-scale priors, a kinetic ordering and a spectral anchor form an explicit identification structure. Across recordings, `r abstract_identifiability(ident)`; the fit diagnostics `r diagnostics_clause(frac_below_d, brief = TRUE, numbers = FALSE)`. Then, `r abstract_prcp(prcp)`; `r abstract_aging(fantasia)`; `r abstract_exercise(exercise)`; and `r abstract_blockade(blockade)`. The states are model-conditional reconstructions, not neural measurements, and how a change is split between them depends on the spectral anchor.

**Keywords**: Heart rate variability; State-space model; Kalman filter; Identifiability; Autonomic nervous system; Integrate-and-fire; Pharmacological blockade

# Introduction

Cardiac autonomic regulation acts on several time scales. The sinoatrial node translates continuous efferent traffic into discrete beats: acetylcholine slows pacemaker firing within seconds, whereas norepinephrine accelerates it over tens of seconds [@kashou2017physiology; @hennis2024pacemaker; @maltsev2023novel; @varzideh2026autonomic]. Postural change or exercise therefore elicits time-resolved responses, namely vagal withdrawal, delayed sympathetic engagement and recovery, whose time courses are of physiological interest [@saul2021heart]. Microneurography measures sympathetic nerve activity directly but is invasive, and the spread of wearable electrocardiographic and photoplethysmographic sensors makes the beat-to-beat (RR) interval series the most accessible observable of this regulation [@rahman2025photoplethysmography]. RR, however, reflects the integrated influence of several processes rather than the activity of either branch [@maltsev2023novel], so recovering the latent dynamics is a problem of inference from an indirect observable [@saul2021heart; @rosas2024bayesian].

Heart rate variability (HRV) analysis summarizes RR with time-domain statistics and spectral measures [@saul2021heart; @liu2025heart; @arya2024multi; @adamczyk2025online]. These descriptors are robust but quantify the output of the system rather than its latent state. From a signal-processing standpoint, three properties of RR limit them: the series is sampled irregularly, at the beats themselves; it is non-stationary during the transients of interest, which violates the assumptions of window-based spectral partitioning [@kim2021ultra; @saul2021heart]; and its low-frequency band mixes sympathetic, vagal and baroreflex influences [@moak2007supine; @liu2025heart]. Generative alternatives model the pacemaker, from multiscale biophysical simulations [@yang2023multiscale; @maltsev2023novel] to integrate-and-fire oscillators in which a phase accumulates at a rate set by autonomic inputs and a beat occurs when it reaches a threshold [@candia2021integral]. For a drift–diffusion phase, intervals follow an inverse Gaussian distribution [@barbieri2005point; @lin2026dynamic], and embedding this first-passage mechanism in a state-space model is usually handled by local linearization, sigma-point filtering or Euler–Maruyama discretization [@rosas2024bayesian; @ding2024high; @amor2018constrained], approximations that can distort the continuous-time dynamics across irregular intervals [@rosas2024bayesian]. Deep-learning models, although effective for pattern recognition, typically do not yield latent variables with explicit physiological meaning.

A second difficulty is identification. If RR is the outcome of a vagal-like process, a sympathetic-like process and observation noise, different combinations of time scales, amplitudes and noise can generate similar interval series [@candia2025robust]. Unconstrained maximum-likelihood estimation can then produce likelihood ridges and solutions in which one process absorbs all variability, so a good fit to RR is necessary but not sufficient evidence of a meaningful decomposition. We therefore treat independent physiological information not as a device to improve fit but as part of the identification structure that defines which solutions are admissible: the characteristic time scales and ordering of vagal and sympathetic effector kinetics [@hennis2024pacemaker; @warner1962mathematical], and the distribution of their modulation across frequency established by pharmacological blockade [@Akselrod1981; @Pomeranz1985; @Taylor1998]. How far these assumptions shape the inferred trajectories should be measured, not assumed.

We implement this strategy in SPARK (Stochastic Phase-domain Autonomic Reconstruction Kinetics). Its components are established, namely Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes [@uhlenbeck1930theory], integrate-and-fire pacing [@candia2021integral], Kalman filtering [@sarkka2020temporal] and spectral partitions of HRV [@Akselrod1981]; the contribution is their combination in three parts. First, a phase-domain conditioning: each recorded interval is treated as a fixed observation window, and a terminal-threshold condition, which approximates first passage closely in the high-drift, low-noise regime of the sinoatrial node [@reith2023approximate], makes the measurement equation linear and Gaussian in the time-integrals of the drives [@hughes2017estimation]. The Kalman filter is then exact, and the transitions across irregular intervals are computed analytically, without discretization. Second, an explicit identification structure, in which time-scale priors, a kinetic ordering and a wavelet-derived spectral anchor define the admissible solutions. Third, a systematic assessment of how far the decomposition is determined by the data and how far by these assumptions, through multi-start identifiability analyses, simulations with known truth and sensitivity analyses, together with an external test against pharmacological blockade and muscle sympathetic nerve activity. To our knowledge this combination has not been applied to RR-interval inference before. The method is available as an R engine and as a browser application that processes recordings locally.

We asked whether RR alone leaves the decomposition under-determined and whether physiological information reduces this ambiguity; whether the states change in the expected direction during orthostatic tilt; how they differ across healthy aging; whether they characterize adaptation and recovery during exercise; and whether they respond to autonomic blockade, and follow sympathetic nerve activity, as their labels imply. Conventional HRV measures and the independent measurements available in subsets of the recordings (tilt angle, arterial pressure, respiration, drug condition and nerve activity) are comparators, not model inputs, and the latent states are reconstructions conditional on the stated assumptions, not measurements of neural activity.

# Methods

Derivations, algorithmic details and the extended justification of the modeling choices are in the supplementary material (section ["Extended methods and discussion"](supplementary.qmd#sec-extended)); the configuration used in every analysis is stored with the results.

## Conceptual model

SPARK represents the sinoatrial node as an integrate-and-fire pacemaker whose drift is modulated by two latent drives. Between two consecutive beats at times $t_{k-1}$ and $t_k$, starting from $\phi(t_{k-1}) = 0$, the sinoatrial phase $\phi$ evolves as a drift–diffusion process,

$$
d\phi(t) = \nu(t)\,dt + \sigma_z\,dW(t), \qquad \nu(t) = \nu_0 - x_p(t) + x_s(t), \qquad t \in (t_{k-1}, t_k],
$$

where $W(t)$ is a standard Wiener process; a beat occurs the first time $\phi$ reaches a normalized threshold of $1$ [@candia2021integral], after which $\phi$ is reset to zero. The drift $\nu(t)$ is the instantaneous pacing rate (Hz), $\nu_0$ the baseline rate, $\sigma_z$ the diffusion coefficient of threshold-level noise, and $x_p(t)$ and $x_s(t)$ the parasympathetic-like and sympathetic-like drives (Hz, deviations from their homeostatic baseline), hereafter the vagal and sympathetic drives for brevity. These labels denote model components distinguished by their kinetics and spectral allocation, not measured neural activity.

## Latent autonomic dynamics

The drives are independent, mean-reverting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes [@uhlenbeck1930theory]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
dx_p(t) &= -\kappa_p x_p(t)\,dt + \sigma_p\,dW_p(t),\\
dx_s(t) &= -\kappa_s x_s(t)\,dt + \sigma_s\,dW_s(t),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\kappa_p$ and $\kappa_s$ are clearance rates (s$^{-1}$) with e-folding times $\tau_p = 1/\kappa_p$ and $\tau_s = 1/\kappa_s$. The diffusion coefficients are parameterized through the stationary variances, $\sigma_b = \sqrt{2\kappa_b V_b}$, with $V_s = \sigma^2_{sys}$ and $V_p = \lambda_P\,\sigma^2_{sys}$, so that $\lambda_P = V_p/V_s$ is the relative vagal variance; the global scale $\sigma^2_{sys}$ leaves the Kalman gain unchanged and is estimated analytically. The state is augmented with the running integrals of the drives, $dI_p = x_p\,dt$ and $dI_s = x_s\,dt$, giving $\tilde{X}(t) = [x_p, x_s, I_p, I_s]^\top$ and $d\tilde{X} = A\,\tilde{X}\,dt + G\,dW$ with constant matrices $A$ and $G$. The transition over any observed interval $\Delta t_k$ is the matrix exponential $\Phi_k = \exp(A\,\Delta t_k)$, with a closed-form process covariance (supplementary sections ["Matrix exponential"](supplementary.qmd#sec-matrix-exponential) and ["Estimation algorithm"](supplementary.qmd#sec-estimation-algorithm)).

## Observation model: phase-domain inversion

Under strict first passage, the interval $T = \inf\{t > 0 : \phi(t) \ge 1\}$ is inverse Gaussian for a constant drift [@barbieri2005point], and a time-varying drift makes the state-space problem nonlinear [@rosas2024bayesian; @ding2024high]. We instead condition on the observed interval and impose that the phase accumulated over $[t_{k-1}, t_k]$ equals one,

$$
1 = \nu_0\,\Delta t_k - \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} x_p(t)\,dt + \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} x_s(t)\,dt + \eta_k ,
$$

where $\eta_k$ is Gaussian threshold-level noise with variance $\sigma_z^2\,\Delta t_k$ and $\sigma_z^2 = \sigma^2_{sys}\lambda_R$. This terminal-threshold condition drops the requirement that $\phi$ stay below 1 within the interval, which is accurate when the drift is large relative to the noise (an explicit bound is given in the supplementary section ["Asymptotic convergence"](supplementary.qmd#sec-phase-mapping)). In the augmented state the observation is linear,

$$
1 - \nu_0\,\Delta t_k = H\,\tilde{X}_k + \eta_k, \qquad H = [0,\ 0,\ -1,\ 1],
$$

so the Kalman recursions are exact. After each measurement update the integral states are reset to zero while $x_p$ and $x_s$ continue to evolve, which represents the restart of phase accumulation at each beat while preserving the memory of the drives across beats. To limit the influence of ectopic beats and detection artifacts, the noise variance at each beat is inflated by a multiplier that grows with the largest relative change between adjacent intervals (supplementary section ["Extended methods and discussion"](supplementary.qmd#sec-extended)); recordings with substantial non-sinus activity are outside the intended scope.

## Model assumptions and identification structure

The physiological information that restricts the admissible solutions is listed in @tbl-identification. These specifications are model assumptions informed by external evidence; they are not estimated from the present data, and their influence is evaluated by the identifiability analyses below.

| Component | Form | Rationale | Default setting |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Positivity and kinetic ordering | $\kappa_s = e^{\theta_1}$, $\kappa_p = \kappa_s + e^{\theta_2}$ | Positive rates; vagal kinetics faster than sympathetic | Structural |
| Time-scale priors | Log-normal on $\tau_p$ and $\tau_s$ | Rapid vagal and slow sympathetic effector kinetics | 95% intervals: $\tau_p$ [3, 6] s; $\tau_s$ [100, 300] s |
| Separation prior | Beta on $U = (\kappa_p - \kappa_s)/(\kappa_p + \kappa_s)$ | Discourages collapse of the two time scales | Mode at $\kappa_p/\kappa_s = 20$; weight 10 |
| Spectral anchor | $\lambda_P$ fixed from partitioned wavelet energy | Allocates variance between branches by frequency | Crossover 0.10 Hz; band 0.04–0.40 Hz; vagal floor fraction 0.25 |
| Timing-jitter prior | Log-normal on equivalent RR timing jitter | Limits absorption of autonomic variance by the noise term | 95% interval [0.5, 20] ms |

: Components of the identification structure {#tbl-identification}

The ordering $\kappa_p > \kappa_s$ removes label switching, that is, a solution in which the fast and the slow process exchange roles. The time-scale priors reflect rapid vagal and slow sympathetic effector kinetics [@hennis2024pacemaker; @warner1962mathematical; @Pomeranz1985; @saul1991transfer] and are fixed across recordings. The ratio $\lambda_P$ is a deterministic function of the global wavelet spectrum of heart rate [@gruszecki2024wavelet; @zhuravlev2025continuous], partitioned into vagal and sympathetic energy with logistic frequency weights that encode pharmacological-blockade evidence [@Akselrod1981; @Pomeranz1985; @Hayano1991; @hopf1995low; @Taylor1998]. Because it is computed from the series being fitted, $\lambda_P$ is data-informed, and equating the ratio of spectral energies with the ratio of latent variances is an approximation (supplementary section ["Spectral anchoring"](supplementary.qmd#sec-spectral-anchor)). The jitter prior, which spans the range expected for electrocardiographic and photoplethysmographic acquisition, limits the extent to which the noise term can absorb autonomic variability.

## Inference and uncertainty

The Kalman recursion, with the Joseph form of the covariance update, processes the intervals sequentially. The baseline $\nu_0$ and the scale $\sigma^2_{sys}$ are profiled out analytically by generalized least squares, using two filters that share one Kalman gain. The remaining parameters $\theta = (\ln\kappa_s,\ \ln(\kappa_p - \kappa_s),\ \ln\lambda_R)$ are estimated by maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation: the negative profiled log-likelihood plus the negative log-prior terms of @tbl-identification is minimized with the Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) algorithm from three starting points, keeping the best run. States are then estimated by forward filtering conditional on the recording-level estimates; because parameter estimation and the spectral anchor use the whole recording, the overall procedure is retrospective rather than strictly causal. The state intervals are conditional on the MAP parameters, and standard errors of $\kappa_p$, $\kappa_s$ and $\lambda_R$ come from the numerical Hessian and the delta method (supplementary section ["Estimation algorithm"](supplementary.qmd#sec-estimation-algorithm)). The model was implemented in R, and a browser implementation with the same specification is available for single recordings (see Code availability).

## Model diagnostics

Filtered tracking accuracy is quantified by the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and the root mean square error (RMSE) between the observed and the implied RR; these are in-sample measures, not prediction errors. If the model is adequate, the standardized innovations $z_k$ are independent standard normal variates, so their probability integral transform $\Phi(z_k)$ is uniform on $(0, 1)$. This was tested with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) distance $D$ against the approximate critical value $1.36/\sqrt{N}$, whose behavior under a correctly specified model was examined by simulation, and serial dependence with the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) of $z_k$ over 40 lags (supplementary section ["Goodness-of-fit diagnostic"](supplementary.qmd#sec-diagnostics)).

## Identifiability analyses {#sec-identifiability-methods}

Four nested specifications were compared (@tbl-specs). All keep the structural constraints of @tbl-identification, and $M_3$, which combines all the physiological information, is used in every other analysis. In $M_0$ and $M_1$, $\lambda_P$ is a free parameter; in $M_2$ and $M_3$ it is fixed by the spectral anchor.

| Specification | Time-scale and separation priors | Spectral anchor ($\lambda_P$ fixed) | Timing-jitter prior |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $M_0$ (RR only) | no | no | no |
| $M_1$ (RR + time-scale constraints) | yes | no | no |
| $M_2$ (RR + spectral evidence) | no | yes | no |
| $M_3$ (combined) | yes | yes | yes |

: Model specifications used in the identifiability analyses {#tbl-specs}

Each specification was fitted from the same `r used("identifiability$n_starts")` dispersed starting points in a deterministic subset of up to `r used("identifiability$max_recordings")` recordings per dataset. For each recording and specification we computed the number of *distinct solutions*; the *near-equivalent fits* (profiled log-likelihood within 2 units of the best) and the dispersion of $\ln\tau_p$, $\ln\tau_s$ and of the reconstructed trajectories among them; the *share of $x_p$ variance* and the proportion of fits in which one process absorbed essentially all variability (share below 0.05 or above 0.95; *one-process collapse*); the proportion of fits inside the 95% prior intervals; and the fit to RR (definitions in the supplementary section ["Identifiability and sensitivity analyses: details"](supplementary.qmd#sec-ident-details)). Because the priors alter the objective, specifications are compared on the profiled log-likelihood and RR error, not on the posterior objective. In addition, profile surfaces of the objective were computed over a $`r used("identifiability$surface_grid")` \times `r used("identifiability$surface_grid")`$ grid of $(\tau_p, \tau_s)$; synthetic series with known drives were fitted in four scenarios (true time scales inside or outside the priors, vagal- or sympathetic-dominant variance); each hyperparameter was varied and each prior component removed in turn; and, to locate the boundary of identifiability, recordings were simulated over the time-scale ratio $\tau_s/\tau_p$ (with $\tau_p$ = `r txt(ident_boundary$settings$tau_p)` s), the variance ratio $\lambda_P$ and the recording length (5, 10 and 30 min) (supplementary section ["Identifiability boundary"](supplementary.qmd#sec-ident-boundary)).

## Data, preprocessing and event definition

*Data and cleaning.* RR intervals were derived from the electrocardiogram (ECG; a Polar H10 chest strap in the exercise cohort), with blood pressure, respiration (Fantasia database) or the tilt angle (Physiologic Response to Changes in Posture, PRCP, database) when available; the model itself uses only RR. RR intervals and covariates were cleaned with an adaptive running-median gate, chosen on simulated series with injected artifacts because it altered about 0.2% of artifact-free beats while correcting about 99.7% of artifacts (supplementary section ["Data preparation and its checks"](supplementary.qmd#sec-data-prep)).

*Participants.* The PRCP database contains ten healthy adults, without reported age or sex. The Fantasia database contains 20 young (21–34 years) and 20 older (68–85 years) healthy adults, with equal numbers of women and men in each group as reported by the database. The exercise cohort consists of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older from the Magallanes region of Chile, whose sample is described in the original study [@castillo2025enhancing]; 263 recordings were analyzed, and the recordings carry no subject characteristics. The blockade dataset comprises seven healthy volunteers, whose age and sex are not given in the public files [@clemson2022beyond].

*Events.* Each tilt and stand-up of the PRCP protocol is analyzed against its own baseline. Onsets came from the tilt-angle signal or the protocol annotations and otherwise, as in the exercise recordings, from piecewise-constant segmentation of heart rate; such events are detected from the modeled RR series, so timing relative to them is not independent evidence about the states (supplementary section ["Event detection"](supplementary.qmd#sec-event-detection)).

## Validation framework: orthostatic perturbation

The first biological test uses the PRCP tilt-table recordings [@heldt2003circulatory]. The expected responses are a fast reduction of the vagal drive after tilt onset and a slower, sustained increase of the sympathetic drive; such a test can show that the components behave coherently, not that they are the autonomic branches. Each maneuver was analyzed against its own baseline (60 to 180 s, beginning 120 s after the previous maneuver returned) and a 120-s recovery window. We computed (i) the change in the mean of each state, standardized by its baseline standard deviation (SD); (ii) whether each change had the expected sign; and (iii) a step-response fit, $x(t) = x_0 + D\,[1 - e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}]$ for $t \ge t_0$, giving the latency, the time constant and the onset lag $t_{0,s} - t_{0,p}$. Between-recording summaries used the median over the tilts of each recording. As a negative control, the same contrast was computed between the two halves of each resting baseline (exact 95% intervals; paired signed-rank test of the absolute standardized changes). Secondary analyses (comparison with a continuous wavelet transform, CWT, moving spectrum; the arterial-pressure response; the dose–response over tilt angle; the responses by kind of maneuver) are in the supplementary section ["Secondary analyses of the perturbation"](supplementary.qmd#sec-analysis-details).

## Generalization: aging

Resting recordings of the Fantasia database [@iyengar1996age] were analyzed in a fixed window (`r window_text(config_used)`), with group membership as the only subject characteristic. The latent summaries were $\nu_0$, $\tau_p$, $\tau_s$, $\ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s)$, $\lambda_P$, $\hat\sigma^2_{sys}$, the equivalent timing jitter, the SD of each state, their ratio and the share of $x_p$ variance. Group differences (older minus young) were summarized by the Hodges–Lehmann shift, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Cliff's $\delta$ with a bootstrap interval, with Benjamini–Hochberg control within each family of variables (latent and conventional HRV); with the group sizes available, all tests are exploratory. Stability was assessed by refitting two non-overlapping windows of each recording, with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(3,1)) of the log values. To examine how far the time constants are set by their priors, both windows were also refitted with weak priors (95% intervals 0.5–60 s and 10–2000 s) and with empirical-Bayes priors estimated on the other half of the subjects (supplementary section ["Partial pooling of the time constants"](supplementary.qmd#sec-pooling)).

## Exercise and recovery

The exercise recordings follow a two-minute step test with a rest–exercise–rest protocol [@castillo2025enhancing]; each is fitted with time-invariant kinetics, so the non-stationary response is carried by the filtered states. The rest level of each state is its mean and SD from 20 s after the start to 5 s before the detected onset; the exercise response is the difference between the mean over the last 15 s of exercise and the rest level; and the path in the $(x_p, x_s)$ plane, with the states $u$ and $v$ in rest-SD units, is summarized by its length, the area it encloses and its maximum quadratic energy $E = (u^2 + v^2)/2$, descriptive measures introduced for this representation. Recovery times used the combination of four candidate definitions and three end-of-exercise rules that scored best on simulated recordings with known recovery constants, with right-censoring and Kaplan–Meier medians (supplementary section ["Recovery-time benchmark"](supplementary.qmd#sec-recovery-benchmark)).

*Perturbation-response descriptors.* As a complement that uses both states and their uncertainty, we computed the descriptors proposed for latent autonomic trajectories [@castillo2026state]: the largest distance from the resting region during the perturbation, the time after its end from which the state stays within that region for 15 s, the probability of such a return within a horizon, and whether a second-stage hidden Markov model places the end of the horizon in a regime other than rest. Distances are in units of the stationary SDs of $M_3$ refitted to the resting beats alone, the tolerance is the 0.999 quantile of the stationary distance, and uncertainty comes from paths drawn from the filtered distributions; their recovery was first checked on simulated recordings with known states (supplementary section ["Perturbation-response descriptors"](supplementary.qmd#sec-descriptors)).

## Pharmacological blockade and sympathetic nerve activity

To test the labels of the two drives against an external manipulation, we used a public dataset in which seven healthy volunteers were studied supine with saline, atropine (0.04 mg/kg), atropine followed by propranolol (0.2 mg/kg; double blockade) and, on a second day, propranolol alone, each condition with 5 min of spontaneous and 5 min of 0.25-Hz paced breathing, and with simultaneous ECG and integrated muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) [@clemson2022beyond; @lancaster2019blocker]. $M_3$ was fitted, unchanged, to every segment, and the stationary SDs of the two drives under each drug were expressed as ratios to saline of the same day and summarized by their geometric mean with a bootstrap 95% interval over volunteers. The expectations were fixed before the first fit: atropine reduces the SD of the vagal-like drive to less than 0.3 of saline in most volunteers, propranolol alone does not reduce it, and double blockade reduces both drives. In the saline period of each session, $M_3$ was also fitted across a hyperventilation and a breath-hold, which raises MSNA, and the changes of the states, heart rate and MSNA from the resting baseline were compared (supplementary section ["Pharmacological blockade and muscle sympathetic nerve activity"](supplementary.qmd#sec-blockade)).

## Conventional HRV comparators and statistical reporting

The SD of RR intervals (SDNN), the root mean square of successive RR differences (RMSSD), mean heart rate, and low-frequency (LF) and high-frequency (HF) power from a tapered periodogram of the resampled tachogram serve as comparators, through rank correlations with the latent summaries and, in the Fantasia recordings, leave-one-out prediction and group discrimination (supplementary section ["Additional analyses of the Fantasia recordings"](supplementary.qmd#sec-fantasia-physiology)). Quantities that vary across recordings are summarized as the median and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range across recordings, which describes dispersion and is not a confidence interval for the median; proportions carry exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% intervals. None of the analyses was preregistered: those on the PRCP, Fantasia and exercise recordings are exploratory, whereas the expectations of the blockade analysis were fixed before its first fit. Random seeds are fixed throughout.

# Results

## RR alone is insufficient for the latent decomposition {#sec-rr-alone}

We first fitted the model without physiological information ($M_0$) from dispersed starting values in `r txt(length(unique(identifiability_metrics$SubjectID)))` recordings drawn from the three datasets; under-determination would appear as solutions with comparable fit to RR but different latent decompositions. `r narrate_identifiability(ident)` The solutions reached from dispersed starting points are shown in @fig-identifiability.

The single solution under $M_3$ is conditional on the spectral anchor and the priors. ## Physiological information reduces solution ambiguity

The specifications are compared in @tbl-ident-metrics on the dispersion of solutions, the stability of the trajectories, the location of the parameters and the RR fit. Improved likelihood is not the criterion, since a well-chosen constraint can reduce ambiguity at a cost in fit; this cost is reported.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ident-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Ambiguity metrics of the multi-start fits by specification (median [2.5th, 97.5th percentile] across recordings; for the two proportions of fits, one-process collapse and fits within the prior intervals, the mean across recordings [2.5th, 97.5th percentile of the per-recording values]). Large upper percentiles of the dispersion of ln $\\tau$ come from recordings in which near-equivalent fits end at vanishingly small or very large time constants, a symptom of the likelihood ridge; they indicate that the fits are not pinned down, not their magnitude."
#| echo: false
if (!is.null(identifiability_metrics)) {
  cols <- c(`Distinct solutions` = "n_solutions",
            `Near-equivalent fits` = "n_equiv",
            `SD of ln $\\tau_p$ (near-equiv.)` = "sd_ln_tau_p_equiv",
            `SD of ln $\\tau_s$ (near-equiv.)` = "sd_ln_tau_s_equiv",
            `Range of $x_p$ variance share` = "share_p_range_equiv",
            `One-process collapse` = "collapse_frac",
            `Within prior intervals` = "frac_in_phys_range",
            `Best RMSE (ms)` = "best_rmse_ms")

  proportion_cols <- c("collapse_frac", "frac_in_phys_range")
  out <- lapply(
      X = c("M0", "M1", "M2", "M3"),
      FUN = function(sp) {
        out <- vapply(
          X = cols,
          FUN = function(cn) {
            x <- identifiability_metrics[spec == sp][[cn]]
            if (cn %in% proportion_cols) {      # a proportion of fits: the mean over recordings (as in the text), not a median that is 0 or 1
              q <- quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
              sprintf("%.0f%% [%.0f%%, %.0f%%]", 100 * mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 100 * q[1], 100 * q[2])
            } else median_range_text(x, 2)
          },
          FUN.VALUE = ""
        )
        out <- list(out)
        setNames(out, sp)
      })

  out <- do.call(cbind, lapply(out, as.data.table))      # one column per specification (works in any data.table version)

  tb <- cbind(Metric = names(cols), out)
  setnames(tb, c("M0", "M1", "M2", "M3"), spec_tex(c("M0", "M1", "M2", "M3")))      # $M_0$ ... $M_3$

  knitr::kable(tb)
} else cat("[PENDING: results/identifiability.rds]")
```


`r narrate_constraints(ident, sensitivity, sim_recovery)`

`r narrate_boundary(ident_boundary)`

For $M_3$, optimization converged for `r n_conv` of `r n_total` recordings (`r pct_conv`%; `r ds_counts`). The filtered reconstruction of RR had an in-sample MAPE of `r mape` and an RMSE of `r rmse`. The innovation diagnostics `r diagnostics_clause(frac_below_d)`: the median KS distance was $D$ = `r ks_dist` against a mean critical value of `r mean_crit_d`, compared with `r txt(if (!is.null(checks)) pct(mean(checks$calibration$KS_Stat > checks$calibration$crit)))` of well-specified simulations exceeding it, and `r pacf_viol` PACF lags lay outside the approximate bounds on average (Supplementary Figure S10). This residual structure plausibly reflects respiratory and baroreflex oscillations that the model does not represent, and the states are conditional on it. The e-folding times were `r taup_mean` (vagal drive) and `r taus_mean` (sympathetic drive), MAP estimates under informative priors and the enforced ordering (supplementary section ["Fit and innovation diagnostics"](supplementary.qmd#sec-fit-diagnostics)).

# Discussion

## Principal observations

We examined whether a physiology-informed state-space model can reconstruct model-conditional autonomic dynamics from RR intervals when the latent decomposition is not identified by RR alone. `r conclusion_identifiability(ident)` In the datasets analyzed, the innovation diagnostics `r diagnostics_clause(frac_below_d, numbers = FALSE)`, so the reconstructions are conditional on a noise model that holds only approximately; with this caveat, `r findings_summary(prcp, fantasia, exercise, inline = TRUE)` Beyond these checks of internal consistency, one external test was possible: in a public blockade dataset, the vagal-like drive behaved as a vagal component, whereas the sympathetic-like drive was not independent of it and did not follow sympathetic nerve activity. The representation is therefore best read as a fast drive with pharmacological support and a slow drive defined by its time scale.

## Physiological meaning and relation to conventional HRV

The latent trajectories are physiologically constrained reconstructions: they describe the drives that the model needs, given its kinetic and spectral assumptions, to account for the observed interval timing, and this is the sense in which the components are called vagal-like and sympathetic-like. `r prcp_discussion_sentence(prcp)` `r blockade_discussion_sentence(blockade)` The path geometry in the $(x_p, x_s)$ plane and the quadratic energy $E$ are descriptive devices, not an energy or a dissipation of the physiological system.

Conventional HRV summarizes how variable RR is; SPARK asks what latent state could account for how RR changes and how that state responds and recovers, so the two are complementary. For signal processing, the representation offers what window-based estimates do not: once the recording-level parameters are fitted, the states are updated at every beat without a stationarity window, irregular sampling is handled exactly, and each state carries an uncertainty interval. Window-based spectral estimates trade temporal against frequency resolution under non-stationarity [@saul2021heart; @kim2021ultra]; the comparison with a CWT moving spectrum (supplementary material) depends on the assumptions of the filter and does not establish general superiority. `r hrv_information_sentence(fantasia, hrv)` Incomplete prediction from a limited set of HRV metrics does not establish incremental clinical value, which requires independent outcomes.

## Identification and physiological priors

In an underdetermined inverse problem, physiological knowledge is part of the identification structure (@tbl-identification), and two consequences follow. First, the kinetic estimates are posterior modes under informative priors that are fixed across recordings: they are regularized toward the priors but not bounded by them, differences in $\kappa$ between groups should be read together with the prior–posterior contrast, and the separation of fast and slow time scales is built into the structure, not an empirical finding. The boundary simulations show that the priors prevent one-process collapse but cannot create identifiability where the time scales overlap. Second, the spectral anchor assigns branch energy by frequency and is computed from the same recording; conditions in which the two branches overlap in frequency, such as strong orthostatic stress or exercise, may lead to misattribution between the drives [@liu2025heart; @menuet2025redefining]. `r blockade_anchor_sentence(blockade)` `r sensitivity_sentence(sensitivity)`

## Phase-domain formulation and relation to existing approaches

Point-process models of heartbeat intervals based on generalized linear structures are largely phenomenological with respect to the sinoatrial node [@barbieri2005point; @chen2012unified], and state-space formulations of integral pulse frequency modulation generally solve the nonlinear first-passage observation in the time domain with extended or unscented filtering [@candia2021integral; @ding2024high; @amor2018constrained]. By conditioning on the observed interval, SPARK obtains a measurement equation that is linear in the integrated drives, together with exact Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transitions across irregular intervals, so the filter is exact and needs no time-stepping approximation; the same structure makes it inexpensive enough to run in a web browser. The price is the terminal-threshold approximation, whose neglected boundary term is bounded in proportion to the ratio of diffusion to the square root of the drift (supplementary material); `r epsilon_sentence(checks)`. Under strict first passage the interval variance also scales with the inverse cube of the drift, a dependence that SPARK does not represent (supplementary sections ["Interval-variance scaling"](supplementary.qmd#sec-heteroskedasticity) and ["Extended methods and discussion"](supplementary.qmd#sec-extended)).

## Limitations

The latent states are model-based reconstructions and not measurements of autonomic neural activity; `r blockade_limitation_sentence(blockade)` The innovation diagnostics `r diagnostics_clause(frac_below_d)`, so the reported intervals are conditional on a noise model that holds only approximately.`r tau_p_limit` Recovery times and time constants are shaped by their priors, and in recordings whose duration is comparable to or shorter than the sympathetic time scale, $\tau_s$ is informed mainly by its prior. The hyperparameters are fixed across recordings, kinetics and variances are constant within a recording, the states are filtered and not smoothed, a better local optimum cannot be excluded for an individual recording, and the simulations use data generated by the model itself. The apportioning of a perturbation-induced change between the two drives depends on the spectral anchor: in the sensitivity analyses the share of latent variance attributed to the vagal-like process changed `r share_sensitivity_clause(sensitivity)`. For the same reason the tonic level of each drive is not identified, because $\nu_0$ and constant offsets of $x_p$ and $x_s$ enter the likelihood only through their combination with the mean rate; comparisons of variability, kinetics and mean rate are supported, but not of absolute vagal or sympathetic tone.

`r kinds_limit_sentence(prcp)` The tilt-table dataset is small (`r prcp_n_text(prcp)`), its tilts are not independent within a recording, and events detected from RR are not independent evidence about the states. Sex and gender were not analyzed: they are not reported for the PRCP and blockade participants or attached to the exercise recordings, and the Fantasia groups are balanced by sex but too small for sex-stratified analyses, so sex differences in the latent dynamics remain untested. The exercise cohort has a single protocol and no clinical outcomes, so the clinical relevance of the trajectories and their behavior in overt autonomic pathology were not evaluated [@braffett2025cardiovascular; @talishinsky2025autonomic]. Finally, the single-stream formulation has no respiratory or blood-pressure inputs: respiratory sinus arrhythmia is captured only within the vagal state and baroreflex feedback is implicit [@seidman2024long; @skytioti2022respiratory; @liu2025heart], so central autonomic commands cannot be distinguished from peripheral mechanical modulation.

## Future directions

Concurrent respiratory and arterial-pressure signals could enter through explicit coupling terms [@tsai2025photoplethysmography; @parikh2025evaluation; @witteveen2025toward], reducing reliance on the spectral anchor; larger blockade studies with graded doses and microneurography [@maki2024integrative; @maciel2025avaliaccao] could calibrate the allocation of low-frequency variance; and hierarchical formulations could learn the hyperparameters across recordings. Datasets with clinical outcomes would show whether the trajectories and their perturbation-response descriptors carry prognostic information, and quantities such as the phase-plane geometry or critical slowing down of the kinetics [@de2024ergodicity; @tirabassi2024linear] could be explored, each requiring dedicated validation.

# Conclusion

SPARK reconstructs latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals with an exact continuous-time filter and an explicit physiological identification structure. In the datasets analyzed, this structure reduced solution ambiguity and one-process collapse at a cost in RR error, and the reconstructed states responded coherently to orthostatic and exercise-related challenges. Under pharmacological blockade the fast drive behaved as a vagal component, whereas the slow drive was not independent of it and did not follow sympathetic nerve activity. SPARK is therefore suited as an interpretable, uncertainty-aware dynamical representation of RR for exploratory and methodological research, in which the fast drive has external support and the slow drive is defined by its time scale. Residual structure, conditional intervals and the dependence of variance allocation on the spectral anchor remain limitations, and interpretation of the components as quantitative measures of parasympathetic and sympathetic activity requires further independent validation.

# Code availability {.unnumbered}

The model is implemented in R (engine deposited with this article as model_code.R). An equivalent implementation runs entirely in the browser, without uploading data, at <https://matcasti.github.io/SPARK-app/>. In the five reference series tested, its likelihood, states and parameter estimates agree with those of the R engine (fitted parameters to within 10^-5^, relative; states, in Hz, to within 10^-6^). The application is intended for research use and exploration, not for clinical decisions.

# Data availability {.unnumbered}

The PRCP recordings (Physiologic Response to Changes in Posture; <https://doi.org/10.13026/C2PC7R>) and the Fantasia database (<https://doi.org/10.13026/C2RG61>) are publicly available from PhysioNet [@goldberger2000physiobank] under the Open Data Commons Attribution license; the repository downloads them with checksum verification (`make download`). The blockade recordings are available from Lancaster University (<https://doi.org/10.17635/lancaster/researchdata/280>, Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial); the repository prepares them from the downloaded file (`make prep`). The RR-interval series of the exercise cohort (263 recordings, without personal identifiers) are in the repository's `data-raw/tmst` folder. The analysis code and its configuration are at <https://github.com/matcasti/SPARK-model/>, and the figures, tables and numbers of this article are regenerated from them (`make data`, `make run`, `make render`). The repository is public and under version control; the version used for this article is the release v1.1.0 (<https://github.com/matcasti/SPARK-model/releases/tag/v1.1.0>), which fixes the code and configuration at a dated commit and carries the result files of the article, whose checksums are listed in the repository (`results/MANIFEST.csv`). The release is not deposited in a repository that issues a DOI.
